1.pericope_label: O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph... He shall choose our inheritance for us, the excellency of Jacob whom he loved

schools.summary: Delitzsch alone names an occasion — Jehoshaphat's bloodless victory, the going up being the ark carried home, and the trumpet making this 'the proper new year's' psalm. Ellicott works from custom and text: the hand-clapping belongs to a coronation, the Septuagint's 'his inheritance' suggests the verse once ran 'He chooses us for His inheritance', and the excellency of Jacob means the country.

Calvin rejects the temple dedication as 'a conjecture which has little to support it' and argues that the deliverance celebrated must be Israel's, since a formidable Gentile kingdom would have given no cause for joy. Gill refers the whole psalm to the ascended Christ and reads the Gentiles as those chiefly summoned.

Clarke divides the reasons for praise between the two audiences — the Jews for the return from Babylon, the Gentiles for their calling — and would rather read the subduing 'in the past tense, relative to what God did for their fathers'; Wesley takes the 'us' of that verse as the church.

Henry allows the summons to be either Israel's or the world's, and defends demonstrative worship against the charge of indecency, since 'God will accept the strength of the affection'. Spurgeon lets Israel lead and the Gentiles follow, and turns the terribleness protective: 'omnipotence, which is terrible to crush, is almighty to protect.'

Augustine reads the title rather than the occasion, taking the sons of Korah through the place of Calvary and the children who mocked Elisha's bald head, so that 'Go up, thou bald head' becomes 'Crucify Him'.

debates.question: What occasion does the psalm belong to?

positions.view: Jehoshaphat's victory over the allied neighbouring nations — 'a victory without a conflict, and consequently all the more manifestly a victory of Jahve'.
Not the temple dedication. More likely a psalm delivered to the Levites 'before the temple was built, and when the ark as yet abode in the tabernacle'.
'The happy state of the Jews when returned to their own land', with the calling of the Gentiles as the spiritual sense.
The ascension of Christ, and the gathering of the Gentiles that followed it.

debates.question: What is the excellency of Jacob?

positions.view: The country — 'literally the loftiness of Jacob', a phrase used elsewhere of the national glory, the Temple, and even 'the pride of Jacob'.
'The presence and worship, and blessing of God.'
God himself: 'he was the boast and glory of Israel, he is and shall be ours'.

outliers.view: The only voice to expound the psalm's title instead of its occasion, deriving from the sons of Korah a whole meditation on the mocking of the Cross.

themes: O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph.
For the Lord most high is terrible; he is a great King over all the earth.
He shall subdue the people under us, and the nations under our feet.
He shall choose our inheritance for us, the excellency of Jacob whom he loved. Selah.

5.pericope_label: God is gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet... For God is the King of all the earth: sing ye praises with understanding

schools.summary: Ellicott settles the going up from the noise — 'not... to heaven, but... to the Temple, as is shown by the public acclaim accompanying the ark' — and reads both musical directions musically: 'strike the harp', and 'play a fine tune', or with the versions 'play with skill'. Delitzsch takes the ascent to presuppose a descent, God having 'come down to fight on behalf of His people'.
Gill will have only the ascension: the Son of God went up 'from earth to heaven in human nature, really, locally, and visibly, in the sight of his apostles'.

Clarke orders the two senses, the ark 'primarily' and the ascension as the general understanding, and turns the qualification into a rule of the mind: 'let sense and sound go together... Understand what you sing; and feel what you understand.' Wesley makes the verse 'literally of the ark: but mystically of Christ's ascension', and asks that praise be sung 'not formally and carelessly, but seriously'.

Henry defends the repetition — 'it is no vain repetition if it be done with new affections' — and distinguishes singing intelligently from singing instructively, since 'it is not an acceptable service if it be not a reasonable service'. Spurgeon paints the triumphal return and turns the same requirement against slovenly and against merely musical worship.

debates.question: Where does God go up to?

positions.view: To the Temple — the ark returning to its resting-place after victory, amid public acclaim.
To heaven, at the ascension of Christ — 'really, locally, and visibly, in the sight of his apostles'.
Both, in order: the ark literally, the ascension mystically.
Skill in the performance: 'rather, play a fine tune', or adverbially, 'play with skill'.
An instructed mind. Sense and sound must go together; the singer must understand what he sings and mean to teach others by it.

outliers.view: The only voice to turn the verse into a critique of church music, condemning slovenly noise and elaborate performance alike — 'what has a sensuous delight in organs, anthems, etc., to do with devotion?'

themes: God is gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet.
Sing praises to God, sing praises: sing praises unto our King, sing praises.
For God is the King of all the earth: sing ye praises with understanding.

8.pericope_label: God reigneth over the heathen: God sitteth upon the throne of his holiness... for the shields of the earth belong unto God: he is greatly exalted

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the shields with the princes and notes that the ancient versions make them, not God, the subject of the verb — 'have been mightily exalted'. Delitzsch reads in the event 'the great fact of the conversion of all peoples', the word for the nobles carrying 'the twofold meaning of generosi'.

Gill takes the reign over the heathen as begun in the first Christian ages and still unfolding, and the princes as gathered 'not against Christ, as at his first coming, but to him'; he reports the alternative rendering 'the willing ones of his people'.

Clarke reads the princes as the free-willed rather than the high-born, argues from the covenant's date that Abraham's people are properly the Gentiles, and locates the throne of holiness in three places at once — heaven, the temple, and 'the hearts of the faithful'. Wesley finds the same universality in the phrasing 'the God of Abraham' rather than 'Abraham'.

Spurgeon distinguishes the secret rule God holds now over idolaters from the acknowledged rule to come, describes an undisputed throne 'never stained with injustice', and sees the gathering as a parliament where 'princes shall rise up to do him honour'.

positions.view: The willing rather than the well-born: 'the voluntary people... those who gladly receive the word of life', noble as the Bereans were noble.
Actual rulers — nobles who 'bow their willing necks to his sway', the shields of the earth by office.
Both senses together, the word carrying 'the twofold meaning of generosi'.

debates.question: Who is greatly exalted in the last clause?

positions.view: On the ancient versions' syntax, the princes: the 'strong ones' become the subject, and 'have been mightily exalted'.
God. 'Great as secular rulers are, God is greater'; the shields belong to him and derive their might from him.

outliers.view: The only voice to give the throne of holiness three locations at once, descending from the heaven of heavens through the temple to the hearts of the faithful.

themes: God reigneth over the heathen: God sitteth upon the throne of his holiness.
The princes of the people are gathered together, even the people of the God of Abraham: for the shields of the earth belong unto God: he is greatly exalted.
